In less than two weeks the video accumulated over 100 million views and generated intense debate.
The wide-ranging responses - including from TIME, the BBC, SBS, VICE, the New Statesman, and the New York Times - touched upon practically every classic argument for and against philanthropy.
While Donaldson's adoring fans saw the act as wholly praiseworthy, others expressed unease and despair, describing the video as "poverty porn" and a "deeply frustrating" reflection of contemporary life.
The eight-minute video opens with Donaldson standing in front of a cheering crowd, declaring he is on a mission to fund cataract surgery for 1,000 people.
Made in partnership with the nonprofit SEE International, the video is a rapid-fire montage of personal stories and post-op reactions, capturing the overwhelming emotions and expressive gratitude of persons after receiving free cataract surgery.
In one post-op scene, a father sees his son's face clearly for the first time until, ironically, his own tears blur his vision.
One young man - who informs Donaldson he has been subscribed to the MrBeast channel for eleven years - receives $50,000 for university fees after his surgery.
The video concludes with Donaldson pledging that they have performed the same surgery for people in Mexico, Honduras, and Indonesia, thus successfully reaching their 1,000-person goal.
It's all masterfully structured, designed to stir your emotions and retain your attention until the very end of the video.
But that's precisely what rang alarm bells for many viewers, whose dread and apprehension lay in witnessing how something so ostensibly heart-warming actually felt grimly dystopian.
As the video itself acknowledges, cataract surgery is cheap, safe, and can enhance the autonomy of many millions across the globe.
In well-functioning societies and with meaningful global solidarity, this would be an utterly mundane practice, easily accessible for all.
Some jokingly observed that Donaldson only aided the vision of 1,000 people to garner more potential viewers of his content.
While Donaldson appears to be a decent person, acting honestly and in good faith, the joke contains a grain of truth.
The resulting core dilemma, in its simplest form, is whether MrBeast is parasitically feeding off entrenched inequalities to build his brand, "exploiting disabled folks for clout and, ultimately, revenue".
Alternatively, is Donaldson generously using his wealth and influence to promote valuable causes that could benefit millions, undertaking acts far more admirable than his contemporaries with similar influence and reach?

Still, there's no denying that the video falls squarely into the problematic territory of "inspiration porn".
Coined by the late Stella Young, the term refers to instances where persons with disabilities are reduced to caricatures, paraded either for their resilience in "overcoming" their differences or as passive subjects waiting for cashed-up abled folk to "cure" them and save the day.
By unabashedly embracing this genre, Donaldson's video proved both surgically precise in knowing what will capture an audience and yet crudely naïve in not anticipating a backlash.
Even the thumbnail - the image displayed for each YouTube video when browsing - feels clumsily manipulative, featuring the heroic benefactor MrBeast with his arm around a child who has tears streaming down their face.
The child does not appear in the video.
Cracking the YouTube code By some distance, Donaldson is the most popular YouTuber on the planet, boasting over 130 million subscribers to his main channel alone, and over 80 million more across his other channels.
In a recent three-month period, his YouTube videos were watched by a staggering 600 million people.
You may not know who he is, but if you have kids or grandkids aged between 6 and 16, they know him and likely love him.
It is hard to overstate how much influence this 24-year-old from North Carolina possesses and the intensity of affection among his many millions of fans.
Arguably, no one understands YouTube better than Donaldson, who regularly confesses that his life has been a singular obsession with the platform after he first began posting videos in 2012.
Revealing an acute insight into what makes for "viral" content - and his sheer relentless determination - Donaldson first found a mass audience through deliberately inane endurance challenges, such as counting to 100,000 in one sitting (which took over 40 hours).
In 2016, Donaldson dropped out of university after only two weeks, reportedly telling his mother that he'd "rather be poor than do anything besides YouTube".
As he gained followers and revenue the same basic formula remained, only drastically scaled up with ever more ambitious and outlandish spectacles.
Today, one way to describe a typical MrBeast video would be "childhood hypotheticals made reality".
That is, Donaldson takes the mind-wandering fantasies of our youth ("Wouldn't it be fun to play hide-and-seek in a shopping mall with 100 people?") and makes it happen.
While most are seemingly fun and lighthearted, or feature Donaldson inflicting suffering on himself, others border on the cruel by exploiting the discomfort people are willing to endure for a cash reward.
It doesn't work for everyone, and many will find a typical MrBeast video to be crass, gauche, extraordinary wasteful, and exhausting to watch.
But like it or not, this manic style has proven incredibly effective, and they have it down to a fine art.
Videos are tightly structured, edited at a frantic pace, smoothly incorporate sponsorships deals, and are stuffed with cross-promotion of the "MrBeast Burger" chain and "Feastables" snack range.
For the uninitiated it can seem like bewildering nonsense, but it's all precisely engineered to maximise engagement.
In interviews he has confessed that "building this business is like cocaine to me.
I just don't know how to stop ...
But, sometimes we gotta splice stuff like this in.
In other words, the decadence is not shamelessly wasteful, but carefully strategic, for it enhances their capacity to achieve more philanthropic ventures in the future.
Suffice to say, this is a fine line to walk.
Donaldson is undoubtedly brilliant, and in a world where influencers like Andrew Tate are corrupting young minds in extraordinarily harmful ways, there are far worse people who could hold the mantle of most popular YouTuber.
Though Donaldson is oddly one-dimensional, with a mask that never drops, his demeanour is always affable and his content is family friendly.
Still, his seeming obsession with growth and reach can manifest in a curious lack of reflection.
This was perhaps most starkly obvious in a video - which cost $3.5 million to produce and has been watched over 360 million times - in which he recreated the Netflix series Squid Game, with 456 contestants competing for $456,000.
Of course, unlike the series, the elimination of contestants did not end with their gruesome deaths.
However, also absent was any recognition of the irony of it all, given Squid Game's blunt commentary on how class disparity enables economically precarious persons to be exploited for the entertainment of the wealthy.
While this depthless quality is mostly harmless
